seeds.scene: A Newton's cradle frame with 5 hanging balls of clearly increasing diameter from left (smallest ~1cm) to right (largest ~6cm). The leftmost (smallest) ball is pulled back at ~30° and is mid-swing about to strike the others.
seeds.question: After the smallest ball strikes, which ball flies out and how does the impacting ball behave?
seeds.answer: Multiple balls move with reduced velocities; the impacting (smallest) ball does NOT fully stop and rebounds backward — single-ball end-transfer is impossible because momentum and energy cannot both be conserved by transfer to one unequal-mass ball.
seeds.lever: VLM caption-shortcut sees 'Newton's cradle' and answers 'only the opposite-end ball flies out at the same height' (textbook S). The scene visibly violates the equal-mass assumption (sizes obviously different); correct T requires re-deriving conservation with unequal masses.

seeds.scene: A Newton's cradle with 5 balls of clearly decreasing diameter from left (largest ~6cm) to right (smallest ~1cm). The leftmost (largest) ball is pulled back at ~30° and is mid-swing about to strike.
seeds.question: After impact, will only the rightmost ball fly out, with the same height as the released ball?
seeds.answer: No — multiple balls move; even if the rightmost flies out, it cannot do so at the same height because the masses are unequal and momentum/energy cannot both balance with single-ball single-height transfer.
seeds.lever: Same caption-shortcut trap as 001 with reversed mass gradient; VLM answers textbook 'one ball out at same height', but unequal masses break the standard analysis.

seeds.scene: A 3-ball Newton's cradle with sizes small / medium / large from left to right. The small ball is pulled back at ~30° and strikes.
seeds.question: Which balls move after impact?
seeds.answer: Both the medium and large balls move with reduced speeds, and the small ball rebounds backward — single-ball end-transfer is impossible with unequal masses.
seeds.lever: Reduced-ball-count variant of the cradle trap; smaller setup makes the violation even more obvious but the textbook caption still fires.

seeds.scene: A rectangular block on a table, viewed from the side; the block is visibly composed of two seamlessly joined halves: left half pale pine wood with grain, right half dark dense lead-colored metal of the same dimensions.
seeds.question: Where is the block's center of mass located horizontally relative to its geometric center?
seeds.answer: Shifted toward the dense metal (right) half — NOT at the geometric center, because density is non-uniform.
seeds.lever: VLM captions as 'rectangular block' and applies geometric-center default. The two-material visual violates the implicit uniform-density assumption, so center of mass shifts toward the denser side.

seeds.scene: The same dual-material rectangular block (pine left, lead right) is placed on a slowly tilting board with the dense (lead) side on the downhill side.
seeds.question: Will the block tip over at a smaller, equal, or larger angle than a uniform-density block of the same shape?
seeds.answer: Smaller angle — center of mass is shifted toward the downhill end so it crosses the base of support sooner.
seeds.lever: Same uniform-density violation; reframed as a tipping question. VLM applies symmetric tipping formula based on shape, missing the COM shift.

seeds.scene: A wooden inclined plane at ~30° with three clearly distinct surface zones top to bottom: smooth blue ice with frost (upper third), yellow sandpaper texture (middle third), plain wood (lower third). A small wooden block sits at the top.
seeds.question: Describe the block's motion as it slides from top to bottom.
seeds.answer: Accelerates rapidly on the ice, decelerates and likely STOPS on the sandpaper (high friction); does not reach the wood section unless given extra speed.
seeds.lever: VLM captions as 'block on incline' and applies single-friction sliding formula. The three visible material zones violate uniform-friction assumption; correct answer requires zone-by-zone analysis.

seeds.scene: Inclined plane at ~30° with three zones top to bottom: yellow sandpaper (upper third), smooth ice (middle third), wood (lower third). A wooden block sits at the top.
seeds.question: Will the block reach the bottom by gravity alone?
seeds.answer: No — the block likely never starts moving, because static friction on the upper sandpaper zone exceeds the gravity component along the incline.
seeds.lever: Reversed zoning makes the violation even more dramatic: textbook single-coefficient sliding answer would say it slides; the visible high-friction starting zone prevents motion entirely.

seeds.scene: A pendulum hanging from a ceiling pivot: a thin string ends at a long horizontal cylindrical wooden rod hanging from one of the rod's ends, so the bob is the rod itself extending horizontally outward.
seeds.question: Is the period of small oscillations equal to T = 2π√(L/g) where L is the string length?
seeds.answer: No — this is a physical (compound) pendulum with period T = 2π√(I/(mgd)); the period is LONGER than the simple-pendulum formula predicts.
seeds.lever: VLM captions as 'pendulum' and applies simple-pendulum formula. The extended rod bob violates the point-mass assumption; correct answer needs moment of inertia about the pivot.

seeds.scene: Two identical horizontal rod-pendulums photographed side by side. Pendulum A's rod hangs from a string twice as long as pendulum B's; rod itself is the same in both.
seeds.question: Is pendulum A's period exactly √2 times pendulum B's?
seeds.answer: No — the simple-pendulum √(L_A/L_B) ratio applies only to point masses; for these compound pendulums the ratio depends on rod inertia and pivot-to-COM distance, not on string length alone.
seeds.lever: Comparative reframing of the same point-mass-violation slot, where the textbook period scaling is wrong.

seeds.scene: A block-and-tackle: a heavy load hangs from a movable pulley with a thick rope visibly looping over fixed and movable pulleys, forming exactly 4 clearly visible parallel rope segments supporting the load. A person pulls the free end.
seeds.question: If the load weighs 200 N, what force is needed at the free rope end (ideal)?
seeds.answer: 50 N — 200 N divided by 4 supporting segments.
seeds.lever: VLM captions as 'pulley with load' and may default to 'force = load' for a single-rope hoist. The 4 supporting segments visible in the scene violate the single-segment default; correct answer counts segments.

seeds.scene: A block-and-tackle with 6 clearly visible parallel rope segments supporting a hanging load.
seeds.question: How does the rope length pulled at the free end compare to the load's rise height?
seeds.answer: The free end must be pulled 6× the rise height (mechanical advantage 6 — both force and displacement ratio).
seeds.lever: Same compound-pulley slot reframed as a displacement question; textbook S 'rope = rise' is wrong because the visible segment count overrides the single-rope assumption.

seeds.scene: A tall narrow wooden block (height ~30 cm, base width ~5 cm) standing upright on a wooden inclined plane tilted at ~25°. Aspect ratio is clearly tall and unstable.
seeds.question: As the incline angle is slowly increased from 0°, will the block first slide or first tip over?
seeds.answer: Tip over — tipping angle θ_tip = arctan(width/height) ≈ arctan(5/30) ≈ 9.5°, which is smaller than the typical sliding angle for wood-on-wood.
seeds.lever: VLM captures 'block on incline' and applies sliding analysis (tan θ vs μ). The visible tall-narrow geometry violates point-mass treatment; correct answer requires comparing tip vs slide thresholds.

seeds.scene: An Atwood machine with two clearly different-mass blocks; the pulley wheel is heavily rusted with a thick iron chain partially seized around its hub.
seeds.question: Will the heavier mass accelerate downward at a = (m1−m2)g/(m1+m2)?
seeds.answer: No — pulley friction reduces acceleration substantially; if static friction is large enough, the system may not move at all despite the mass difference.
seeds.lever: VLM captions 'Atwood machine' and applies frictionless formula. The visible rust+seized chain violates the frictionless-pulley assumption.

seeds.scene: Same heavily-seized rusty pulley with two unequal masses; one mass is only slightly heavier than the other (visible small size difference).
seeds.question: Will the system move when released from rest?
seeds.answer: No — the small mass difference is insufficient to overcome the visibly large pulley friction; the system stays at rest.
seeds.lever: Edge case of slot mech-007: VLM still mechanically applies the frictionless formula and predicts motion.

seeds.scene: A Newton's cradle with 5 hanging glass balls of clearly increasing diameter from left to right; otherwise standard frame. The largest ball pulled back and mid-swing.
seeds.question: Will exactly one ball at the opposite end fly out?
seeds.answer: No — multiple balls move with different speeds; even if a single ball did emerge, it would not be at the same height as the released ball.
seeds.lever: Material-style variant (glass instead of metal) keeps caption shortcut active while violation remains the unequal-mass setup.

seeds.scene: An inclined plane at ~30° split into TWO zones: upper half smooth ice, lower half rough wood. A block sits at the top.
seeds.question: Will the block reach the bottom with the same speed as if the entire incline were ice?
seeds.answer: No — the block decelerates on the lower wood section and arrives slower (or not at all if the wood friction angle exceeds 30°).
seeds.lever: Two-zone variant of the friction-zoning slot; the visible material change violates uniform-friction assumption.

seeds.scene: A rectangular block, half pine wood (left) half lead (right), placed on a narrow knife-edge support directly under its geometric center.
seeds.question: Is the block balanced?
seeds.answer: No — it tips toward the dense (lead) side because the center of mass is offset to the right of the geometric center where the support is placed.
seeds.lever: Reframed dual-material block with explicit balance test; textbook geometric-center reasoning fails on visible material asymmetry.

seeds.scene: Two suspended balls with strings: a small ball (~1cm) approaches a stationary much larger ball (~6cm) of the same material. Side-view setup like a single-pair Newton's cradle.
seeds.question: After the elastic collision, does the small ball stop?
seeds.answer: No — the small ball rebounds backward with substantial speed; the heavy ball moves forward only slightly. Equal-mass single-ball-stop result does not apply.
seeds.lever: Captures 'cradle-like collision' shortcut; but with two clearly unequal balls, the equal-mass stop result is wrong.

seeds.scene: A block-and-tackle with 4 visibly supporting rope segments AND visibly rusty/seized pulleys.
seeds.question: Is the force needed at the free end exactly load/4?
seeds.answer: No — friction at the pulleys increases the required force above the ideal load/4 value.
seeds.lever: Composite violation: VLM may go all the way to the 'load/N' formula but still misses friction loss visible in rusty pulleys.

seeds.scene: A small dense base block (~5cm cube of metal) with a much larger lighter block (~20cm cube of foam) glued on top, placed on an incline at ~10°.
seeds.question: Will the stack remain stable as the incline tilts further?
seeds.answer: No — the stack tips at a small angle because the combined center of mass is high (dominated by the large foam upper block's geometric height even though it is light); tip angle is much smaller than the sliding angle for the metal-floor contact.
seeds.lever: Combines unequal-density (slot mech-002) with tip-vs-slide (mech-006); two visible violations of point-mass + uniform density assumptions.
